summary:
A.S.T.R.A. developed by Dino Labs, is an autonomous onboard medical hub (Edge Computing) designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions—from Low Earth Orbit (ISS) and lunar bases to deep-space transit toward Mars.

Addressing the five hazards identified by the NASA Human Research Program (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments), A.S.T.R.A. eliminates reliance on real-time ground telemedicine, which faces up to 40-minute round-trip communication delays and Deep Space Network blackouts.

Instead of introducing new hardware, A.S.T.R.A. fuses native spaceflight telemetry—the Astroskin biometric vest, ECLSS cabin atmosphere and radiation sensors, periodic biological panels, and a built-in cognitive battery (PVT & PANAS)—into a dynamic 14-day rolling baseline and a weighted Crew Readiness Index. The software guides astronauts through immediate countermeasures (shielding protocols, personalized nutrition rations, adaptive exercise, and coherent breathing) while generating encrypted, SHA-256-verified daily medical reports relayed asynchronously to ground flight surgeons.
details:
A.S.T.R.A. (Astronaut Smart Tracking and Risk Analysis), developed by Dino Labs, is an onboard health-monitoring application that lets astronauts track and manage their own health autonomously during long-duration missions beyond Low Earth Orbit, where real-time support from Earth is not available.

It turns raw telemetry from Astroskin biometric sensors into clear guidance: it learns each astronaut's personal 14-day baseline, flags significant deviations such as an HRV drop of more than 20%, and combines sleep, recovery, cognitive performance, physical activity, and nutrition into a single Crew Readiness Index from 0 to 100. When the index falls below 50, high-risk tasks such as spacewalks are locked as a preventive measure.

The app also cross-checks health data against life-support telemetry, for example to tell psychological stress apart from the effects of high cabin CO2, and projects trends 48 hours ahead while guiding crews through immediate countermeasures (emergency storm-shelter and CO2-purge alerts, diet-filtered nutrition rations, and coherent breathing).

The main benefit is fewer false alarms and earlier detection, because alerts are based on the individual rather than on Earth-based thresholds, and the intended impact is to make crews medically self-sufficient on missions to the Moon and Mars. We built it as an offline-capable Progressive Web App using React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion, with serverless WebRTC peer-to-peer synchronization between onboard tablets and browser APIs for audio, speech, webcam capture, and SHA-256 report verification.

Its creativity lies in reproducing real mission conditions: crew devices sync over an onboard mesh network, while the Flight Surgeon on Earth receives a daily medical report through a delay-tolerant queue that simulates communication latency and blackouts, and can send prescriptions back.

Throughout the design, our team considered alert fatigue, communication delays, the absence of connectivity, hands-free use in emergencies, and data integrity: if a sensor disconnects, the app shows "N/A" instead of simulated values.
